title: June 2015 (Paper II)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (50/50 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Matthew Arnold, Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Matthew Arnold’s “touchstones” were “short passages, even single lines” of classic poetry
beside which the lines of other poets may be placed in order to detect the presence or absence
of high poetic quality.  In his “Study of Poetry” Arnold cited “touchstones” from such
non-English poets as Homer and Dante and also from the English poets, Shakespeare and
Milton.  Which English poet did he disapprovingly call “not one  of the reat classics” in the
list below ?
items.explanation: In 'The Study of Poetry' (1880), Matthew Arnold praised Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, and Milton as high classic poets, but famously judged Geoffrey Chaucer as lacking 'high poetic seriousness', concluding he was not among the supreme classics.

items.title: Q2 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Samuel Pepys
items.stem: Samuel Pepys began his diary on __________.
items.explanation: Samuel Pepys began keeping his famous private diary on 1 January 1660 (New Year's Day 1660), recording significant historical events of Restoration England including the Great Plague and the Great Fire of London.

items.title: Q3 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Peter Ackroyd, W. B. Yeats
items.stem: On which of the following authors has Peter Ackroyd NOT written a biography ?
items.explanation: Peter Ackroyd is a renowned British biographer who authored acclaimed biographies of Charles Dickens (1990), William Blake (1995), and T. S. Eliot (1984), but he did not write a biography of W. B. Yeats (whose definitive biography was written by R. F. Foster).

items.title: Q4 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · W. H. Auden, Louis MacNeice, Stephen Spender
items.stem:
Which roup of the following poets was called the Auden Group because they developed a
style and viewpoint similar to that of W. H. Auden ?
options: Louis MacNeice, C. D. Lewis, Stephen Spender
John Masefield, Edwin Muir, Norman McCaig
MacDiarmid, G. M. Hopkins, Edwin Muir
W. H. Davies, Robert Bridges, John Masefield
items.explanation: The Auden Group (or the 1930s 'Macspaunday' generation) comprised W. H. Auden and his Oxford contemporaries Louis MacNeice, Cecil Day-Lewis, and Stephen Spender, who shared leftist political sympathies and modernist poetic idioms.

items.title: Q5 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
When one line of poetry runs into the next, with no punctuation to slow the reading, it is a
case of __________.
items.explanation: Enjambment is the continuation of a sentence or syntactic unit across a poetic line break without terminal punctuation, propelling the reader forward without pause into the subsequent line.

items.title: Q6 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the Victorian Age ?
options: The rise of a highly competitive industrial technology
An emphasis on strictly controlled social behaviour
A romantic focus on home and family
The rowth of rural traditions and movement from large cities
items.explanation: The Victorian Age was characterized by massive urbanization and the drift of rural populations into industrial factory cities; rural traditions declined rather than grew as urban manufacturing centers expanded.

items.title: Q7 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Sir Walter Scott
items.stem:
In The Heart of Midlothian, Walter Scott deals with real political and personal details, but
notable among his characters is the depiction of __________.
items.explanation: In Sir Walter Scott's Waverley novel The Heart of Midlothian (1818), the heroic protagonist Jeanie Deans walks to London to seek a royal pardon for her sister Effie and famously pleads her case before Queen Caroline, consort of King George II.

items.title: Q8 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Chaucer’s first work, The Book of the Duchess  is a dream poem on the death of __________.
items.explanation: Chaucer's dream-vision elegy The Book of the Duchess (c. 1368) was composed on the death of Blanche of Lancaster, the first wife of Chaucer's royal patron John of Gaunt.

items.title: Q9 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Charles Lamb
items.stem: What was Charles Lamb’s connection with India ?
options: He was fascinated by the Indian jugglers and trades-people in London and wrote an essay on them
He was fascinated by Eastern mystical religions, especially Buddhism
He was a clerk for thirty three years in the East India Company
He was clerk in South Sea House that prepared patents and documents for British trading companies in India
items.explanation: Romantic essayist Charles Lamb worked as a dedicated clerk at the Accountant's Office of the British East India Company in East India House, London, for thirty-three years from 1792 until his retirement on pension in 1825.

items.title: Q10 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II · Northrop Frye, Georg Lukacs, Raymond Williams
items.stem: Find the odd one among the Marxist critics below :
items.explanation: Northrop Frye was a pioneering Canadian theorist of archetypal and myth criticism (famous for Anatomy of Criticism), whereas Georg Lukacs, Louis Althusser, and Raymond Williams are prominent Marxist literary theorists.

items.title: Q11 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
In the lines “With old jewels cover every part, /And hide with ornaments their want of art”
(Essay on Criticism), Pope rejects
items.explanation: In An Essay on Criticism (1711), Alexander Pope satirizes shallow poets who substitute flashy, superficial ornament for genuine poetic substance, rejecting false artificiality in favor of adhering to Nature.

items.title: Q12 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The opposite of hyperbole is __________.
items.explanation: Meiosis is intentional poetic understatement that belittles or downplays the gravity of something, functioning as the direct rhetorical opposite of hyperbole (extravagant exaggeration).

items.title: Q13 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit III: Fiction, short story
items.stem: What significance do we attach to the publication of I Am an Indian in Canada ?
options: The title refers to the autobiography of an unknown Indian writer longing for the South Asian countryside
The first ever account of ethnic conflicts within Canada
The first anthology of Native Canadian writing following the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s
The first anthology of writers afflicted by class and ender differences in Canada of the late 1970s
items.explanation: Published in 1969 and edited by Kent Gooderham, I Am an Indian was the seminal first national anthology of Canadian First Nations / Native writing, marking a vital moment in Canadian indigenous literary sovereignty.

items.title: Q14 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: What is the moral of “The Nun’s Priest’s Tale” ?
options: Slow and steady wins the race.
Greed is the root of all evil.
items.explanation: In Chaucer's 'The Nun's Priest's Tale', the proud rooster Chauntecleer escapes the hungry fox Don Russel by learning never to close his eyes and succumb to the flattery of deceitful tricksters.

items.title: Q15 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · George Eliot
items.stem: The author of the essay “Silly Novels by Lady Novelists” is __________.
items.explanation: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans) published her scathing critical review essay 'Silly Novels by Lady Novelists' in the Westminster Review in October 1856, attacking formulaic, melodramatic popular fiction by Victorian women writers.

items.title: Q16 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Daniel Defoe
items.stem:
The unquenchable spirit of Robinson Crusoe struggling to maintain a substantial existence
on a lonely island reflects __________.
options: man’s desire to return to nature
the aristocrat’s disdain for the harsh social reality
items.explanation: As classic economic and literary theorist Ian Watt argued in The Rise of the Novel (1957), Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719) epitomizes the spirit of homo economicus and the industrious, self-reliant ideals of the rising English bourgeoisie.

items.title: Q17 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Who is the author of the collection The Celtic Twilight ?
items.explanation: The Celtic Twilight (1893) is an enchanting collection of Irish folkloric tales, visionary stories, and essays compiled by W. B. Yeats, giving its name to the early phase of the Irish Literary Revival.

items.title: Q18 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
In medieval England a __________was understood to be a trained craftsman, one who
worked under a master who owned the business.
items.explanation: Under the medieval English guild hierarchy, a journeyman was a qualified craftsman who had completed his apprenticeship and was paid daily wages to work under an established master artisan before earning the status to run his own business.

items.title: Q19 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem:
Christopher Marlowe’s heroes are said to be larger than life, exaggerated both in their faults
and in their qualities.  They have a desire for everything in extreme.  In one of his plays the
hero wants to conquer the whole world.  The name of the play is __________.
items.explanation: In Christopher Marlowe's tragedy Tamburlaine the Great (1587), the Scythian shepherd Tamburlaine displays an insatiable overreaching lust for worldly power and territorial conquest across Asia and the Mediterranean.

items.title: Q20 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Keats
items.stem: With what does the speaker claim to be half in love in “Ode to a Nightingale” ?
options: the scented flavour of early summer
the night sky and all the stars
the peace that comes with death
items.explanation: In stanza 6 of 'Ode to a Nightingale' (1819), John Keats confesses: 'Darkling I listen; and, for many a time / I have been half in love with easeful Death', yearning for peaceful release from mortal suffering.

items.title: Q21 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Aristotle
items.stem:
In wwhich wchapter wof Poetics does wAristotle wuse wthe wword ‘catharsis’ win whis wdefinition wof
tragedy ?
items.explanation: Aristotle presents his canonical formal definition of tragedy and introduces the concept of catharsis (the purgation of pity and fear) in Chapter VI of Poetics.

items.title: Q22 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · T. S. Eliot, Matthew Arnold, Terry Eagleton
items.stem:
Match the following :
(a)
“The Function of Criticism”
(i)
Terry Eagleton
(b)
“The Function of Criticism at
(ii)
Richard Ohmann
the Present Time”
(c)
The Function of Criticism : From
(iii)
Matthew Arnold
‘The Spectator’ to Poststructuralism
(d)
“The Function of English at the
(iv)
T. S. Eliot
Present Time”
The right matching according to the code is :
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: T. S. Eliot wrote 'The Function of Criticism' (1923), Matthew Arnold wrote 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time' (1864), Terry Eagleton authored The Function of Criticism: From 'The Spectator' to Post-Structuralism (1984), and Richard Ohmann wrote 'The Function of English at the Present Time' (1970).

items.title: Q23 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas More
items.stem: Identify the TRUE statement on Thomas More’s Utopia.
options: Utopia is divided into four parts, each dealing with Raphael Hythloday’s adventures in the four suburbs of Antwerp.
Utopia is divided into two parts; the first records a conversation between Thomas More and Raphael Hythloday, and the second is Hythloday’s discourse on the institutions and practices of Utopia.
Utopia is divided into two parts; the first is Thomas More’s discourse on the institutions and practices of Utopia, and the second a conversation between More and Hythloday.
Utopia is divided into four parts, each dealing with the ordered patterns of towns and cities in Antwerp.
items.explanation: Thomas More's Utopia (1516) comprises two distinct books: Book I consists of a dialogue between More, Peter Giles, and Raphael Hythloday debating English social ills, while Book II is Hythloday's comprehensive monologue describing the utopian island commonwealth.

items.title: Q24 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem: In “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner” what disaster befalls the ship and the crew ?
options: The ship is caught in ice and breaks into pieces.
A fierce storm batters the ship and drowns the crew.
“Slimy things with legs” attack the ship and kill many of the crew.
The ship is becalmed and the crew dies of thirst.
items.explanation: After the Mariner shoots the Albatross in Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner', the ship enters the doldrums and is becalmed under a burning sun, causing all two hundred sailors to perish agonizingly of thirst.

items.title: Q25 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Falstaff is a character in __________.
(a)
Henry IV Part I
(b)
The Merry Wives of Windsor
(c)
The Comedy of Errors
(d)
Titus Andronicus
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: Sir John Falstaff is Shakespeare's celebrated comic knight who appears in Henry IV Part 1, Henry IV Part 2, and The Merry Wives of Windsor (and whose death is reported in Henry V).

items.title: Q26 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Virginia Woolf
items.stem:
In her essay “Professions for Women” Virginia Woolf finds an analogy between the act of
writing and __________.
items.explanation: In her 1931 speech 'Professions for Women', Virginia Woolf compares the imaginative novelist to a fisherwoman seated on the bank of a deep lake, casting her line into the unconscious waters until the imagination strikes submerged rock.

items.title: Q27 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean & Caroline · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: The ascension of King James I in __________ inaugurated the Jacobean age.
items.explanation: Following the death of Queen Elizabeth I in 1603, King James VI of Scotland ascended the English throne as King James I, unifying the English and Scottish crowns and inaugurating the Jacobean era (1603–1625).

items.title: Q28 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Lord Byron
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT true of the Byronic hero ?
items.explanation: The Byronic hero (exemplified by Manfred, Lara, and Childe Harold) is brooding, moody, passionate, and tortured by secret guilt, but fiercely unrepentant, refusing to bend or beg for forgiveness.

items.title: Q29 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Thomas Hardy
items.stem:
Like many other novelists, Hardy employed language variation (dialect and standard) with
a purpose.  In this respect which of the following statements is correct ?
options: His major characters such as Tess and Jude always speak in local dialects, as per their social positions.
His major characters such as Tess and Jude rarely speak in local dialects, in spite of their social positions.
His major characters such as Tess and Jude rarely speak in standard language in spite of their social positions.
His major characters such as Tess and Jude rarely speak in a mixture of a dialect and standard.
items.explanation: Thomas Hardy deliberately allocated standard English to tragic protagonists like Tess Durbeyfield and Jude Fawley to emphasize their interior complexity and social mobility, reserving rich Dorset dialect largely for peripheral rustic chorus figures.

items.title: Q30 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Martin Amis
items.stem:
“It used to be said,” began a famous English writer, “everyone had a novel in them ... Just
now, though, in 1999, you would probably be obliged to doubt the basic proposition: What
everyone has in them, these days, is not a novel but a memoir”.  Identify the source :
options: John Fowles, The French Lieutenant’s Woman
items.explanation: Martin Amis opens his celebrated 2000 autobiographical memoir Experience with this exact reflection, noting that by 1999 the universal human impulse had shifted from harboring an unwritten novel to producing a personal memoir.

items.title: Q31 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem: The opening sixteen lines of Paradise Lost comprise :
items.explanation: Milton opens Book I of Paradise Lost with a magnificent 16-line periodic sentence invocation ('Of Man's First Disobedience... Sing Heav'nly Muse...') that builds to line 16 ('Things unattempted yet in prose or rhyme').

items.title: Q32 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean & Caroline · Unit II: Poetry · John Donne
items.stem: Who among the following poets compared human tears to “love’s wine” ?
items.explanation: In John Donne's metaphysical love lyric 'Twicknam Garden', the distraught lover invites disappointed suitors: 'Hither with crystal vials, lovers come, / And take my tears, which are love's wine'.

items.title: Q33 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Samuel Butler
items.stem: Ernest Pontifex is a character in __________.
items.explanation: Ernest Pontifex is the autobiographical protagonist of Samuel Butler's satirical Victorian Bildungsroman The Way of All Flesh (published posthumously in 1903), tracing his struggle against ecclesiastical hypocrisy.

items.title: Q34 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem:
In which of the following stories does Rudyard Kipling present a newspaper editor who
recounts his dealings with a couple of “loafers” ?
items.explanation: Rudyard Kipling's 1888 novella 'The Man Who Would Be King' is narrated by an Anglo-Indian newspaper editor in Lahore who recounts his extraordinary dealings with two British rogue adventurers, Peachey Carnehan and Daniel Dravot.

items.title: Q35 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Thom Gunn
items.stem:
Trying to capture the upbeat mood of 1964-65, the poet Thom Gunn said: “They stood for a
great optimism, barriers seemed to be coming down all over, it was as if World War II had
finally drawn to close, there was an openness and high-spiritedness and relaxation of mood”.
Who were “they” ?
items.explanation: Thom Gunn reflected on the cultural revolution of the mid-1960s British youth culture, identifying The Beatles as the cultural icon that broke down social barriers and embodied new optimistic liberation.

items.title: Q36 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem: In Paradise Lost Milton presents the action of the fall of man in two stages in Books __________.
items.explanation: In Milton's Paradise Lost, Satan's initial psychological assault on Eve occurs in Book IV (whispering into her ear in the toad-dream), which prepares the final catastrophe and actual eating of the fruit in Book IX.

items.title: Q37 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Jonathan Swift
items.stem: In Gulliver’s Travels Struldbruggs are __________.
options: people persecuted by pets and servants.
people lured by a new ideal.
items.explanation: In Part III of Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), the Struldbruggs of Luggnagg are born with a mark on their foreheads signifying immortality; however, they continue to age normally and suffer decrepit, miserable senility without physical release.

items.title: Q38 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Margaret Atwood, William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Margaret wAtwood whas wtried wa wrevisionist wwriting wof wa wcrucial wscene win wHamlet wcalled
“Gertrude Talks Back”.  The scene in Atwood opens with a reference to the name of an
implied listener.   Who is this implied listener ?
items.explanation: Margaret Atwood's revisionist feminist story 'Gertrude Talks Back' (from Good Bones, 1992) features Queen Gertrude talking back to Hamlet in her closet, opening with Gertrude addressing her son Hamlet by name.

items.title: Q39 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Johnson
items.stem: Samuel Johnson wrote London in imitation of __________.
items.explanation: Samuel Johnson published London (1738) as a verse satire composed in imitation of Juvenal's Third Satire (depicting the corruption, crime, and poverty of metropolitan city life).

items.title: Q40 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Buchi Emecheta, Bessie Head
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT written by Buchi Emecheta ?
items.explanation: A Question of Power (1973) is a celebrated novel by the South African-born writer Bessie Head; The Joys of Motherhood (1979), Second-Class Citizen (1974), and Kehinde (1994) are all major novels by Nigerian author Buchi Emecheta.

items.title: Q41 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Johnson, Abraham Cowley
items.stem: Samuel Johnson’s use of the term “metaphysical” in a piece of criticism was __________.
items.explanation: In his Life of Cowley (1779), Dr. Samuel Johnson used the term 'Metaphysical poets' critically and disapprovingly, famously censuring their tendency where 'the most heterogeneous ideas are yoked by violence together'.

items.title: Q42 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Charlotte Bronte
items.stem: “I am not an angel ..... and I will not be one till I die: I will be myself.”  This is __________.
options: Maggie Tulliver in Mill on the Floss
Aurora Leigh in the eponymous poem
Jane Eyre in the eponymous novel
Betty Higdon in Our Mutual Friend
items.explanation: In Chapter 24 of Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre (1847), Jane fiercely asserts her moral and spiritual autonomy to Mr. Rochester when he idolizes her as an otherworldly seraph, replying: 'I am not an angel... and I will not be one till I die: I will be myself.'

items.title: Q43 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit I: Drama · Joe Orton
items.stem: Who among the following playwrights was the son of a ardener ?
items.explanation: British playwright Joe Orton was born in Leicester in 1933 to William Orton, a municipal borough gardener, and Elsie Orton, a machinist and charwoman.

items.title: Q44 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit I: Drama · Richard Brinsley Sheridan
items.stem: “He is the very pineapple of politeness!”  This sentence is an example of __________.
items.explanation: Mrs. Malaprop in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's comedy The Rivals (1775) mistakenly uses 'pineapple' instead of 'pinnacle', serving as the quintessential example of malapropism (ludicrous misuse of a word sounding like the intended one).

items.title: Q45 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language: Basic concepts, theories and pedagogy. English in Use. · Ferdinand de Saussure
items.stem: Ferdinand de Saussure argued that meaning is enerated through __________.
options: a system of structured differences in language
a system of random differences in language
a system of structured references in language
a system of random references in language
items.explanation: Ferdinand de Saussure argued in Course in General Linguistics (1916) that language is a system of structured relational differences with no positive terms, wherein linguistic signs derive meaning purely from their contrastive differences with other signs.

items.title: Q46 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit I: Drama · Arnold Wesker
items.stem: Identify the roup known as “The Wesker Trilogy” ?
options: The Growth of the Soil, Game of Life, In the Grip of Life
Chicken Soup with Barley, Roots, I’m Talking about Jerusalem
The Four Seasons, Chips with Everything, Golden City
Lunatics and Lovers, The Patriots, Dead End
items.explanation: The Wesker Trilogy by British playwright Arnold Wesker comprises Chicken Soup with Barley (1958), Roots (1959), and I'm Talking about Jerusalem (1960), chronicling the political and emotional lives of the Jewish socialist Kahn family.

items.title: Q47 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit I: Drama · Derek Walcott
items.stem: Who is the central character of Derek Walcott’s Dream on the Monkey Mountain ?
options: Diana Guinness, one of the Mitford Sisters
items.explanation: In Derek Walcott's masterpiece Dream on the Monkey Mountain (1970), the central protagonist is Makak, an impoverished and visionary West Indian charcoal burner who experiences hallucinations of an elusive White Goddess.

items.title: Q48 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem: The phrase “darkness visible” (Paradise Lost, 1.63) is an example of __________.
items.explanation: In Milton's Paradise Lost (1.63), the description of Hell's flames that provide 'No light, but rather darkness visible' is a classic oxymoron, juxtaposing two contradictory sensory ideas to convey infernal gloom.

items.title: Q49 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Sam Selvon, Timothy Mo, Hanif Kureishi
items.stem:
What wis wcommon wto wwriters wsuch was wSam wSelvon (The Lonely Londoners), wTimothy wMo
(Sour Sweet), and Hanif Kureishi (The Black Album) ?
options: All of them are brilliant writers of autobiographies who tell stories and write poetry.
They use Standard English with some Creole inflections peculiar to the Caribbean.
They are diasporic writers who depict postcolonial London very different from its colonial representations.
They contrast the ‘First Nations’ with local populations of their respective countries.
items.explanation: Sam Selvon (Trinidadian), Timothy Mo (Anglo-Chinese), and Hanif Kureishi (British-Pakistani) are all diasporic multicultural authors whose fiction depicts London from the vibrant, complex perspective of postcolonial migrant communities.

items.title: Q50 · June 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · F. R. Leavis, Q. D. Leavis
items.stem:
F. R. Leavis and Q. D. Leavis launched a critical journal devoted to the moral centrality of
English Studies.  Name the Journal.
items.explanation: F. R. Leavis and Q. D. Leavis founded and edited the highly influential critical quarterly Scrutiny at Cambridge from 1932 to 1953, championing the supreme moral seriousness and cultural necessity of literary analysis.
